The user came down with a heavy cold in late March and wanted to understand what their numbers were doing. Resting heart rate sat about eight beats above their usual baseline for five consecutive nights, and heart-rate variability fell to roughly two thirds of the thirty-day average on the worst night. Sleep duration was not unusually short but the proportion spent in deep sleep dropped noticeably, and they reported waking repeatedly with a dry throat. They asked whether they should keep training through it. The discussion landed on treating the elevated resting heart rate as the signal to watch rather than the variability figure on any single night, because a single night is noisy and an infection shows up as a run of nights rather than one bad one. They agreed to drop all intensity while the resting heart rate stayed elevated, keep walking, and only return to intervals once it had come back to baseline for two nights in a row. They also noted that the last time they trained through a cold, in the previous autumn, the illness dragged on for well over a fortnight, which was the experience that made them willing to stop this time. Hydration and an earlier bedtime were the two habits they chose to hold on to while recovering, and they set a reminder to revisit the plan after a week.
Recommendation feedback: hard interval session proposed twice and declined both times; the second time marked as too demanding for the day.
Habit hypothesis over 90 days: on evenings with alcohol the next morning's recovery score is lower on average; the sample is small and this is an association, not a cause.
